# Introduction to 1 Chronicles

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of the book of 1 Chronicles

1. Genealogies (ancestor lists) leading from Adam to David and Saul
    1. From Adam to the descendants of Isaac’s son Esau (1:1–54)
    2. The descendants of Isaac’s son Israel (2:1–7:40), including David (2:15, 3:1–9)
    3. The genealogy and death of Saul (8:1–40, 9:35–44, 10:1–14)
    4. Israelites who returned from exile in Babylon (9:1–34)
2. The reign of King David (11:1–29:30)
    1. Warriors who supported David (11:1–12:40)
    2. How David became established and made Jerusalem a sacred place (13:1–17:27)
    3. How David and his warriors defeated Israel’s enemies (18:1–20:8)
    4. How David establish worship arrangements for the Israelites (21:1–29:30)

### What is the book of 1 Chronicles about?

The book of 1 Chronicles is the first part of a history of David and his descendants who were kings of Israel and Judah. The book first situates David’s ancestry among all of the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It then relates the death of Saul, Israel’s first king, and it tells how David became the next king. It describes David’s military triumphs and his preparations for a temple in Jerusalem. It ends with his death. This history continues through the book of 2 Chronicles, which describes David’s successors up to the time of the Babylonian exile. (The books of Ezra and Nehemiah continue this story further and tell what happened after the return from exile.)

This entire history was compiled and composed after the Judeans returned from exile in Babylon. It is designed to show the restored community that it can still fulfill the purposes that Yahweh has for it as his chosen people. So it begins with a long series of genealogies (ancestor lists) that start with Adam, the first man, and trace the branches of his descendants down through key figures such as Noah, Abraham, Jacob, and Judah. The design is to show how Yahweh chose people in various historical periods to further his purposes. This leads ultimately to David. The book describes at length the special role he had in helping the Israelite community live in peace and safety and become centered on the worship of Yahweh.

The message is one of encouragement for the returned exiles. It may have been difficult for them to think of themselves as a distinctive community. They were still ruled by a foreign emperor, and their cities and their temple were in ruins. But the book stresses that if they will worship Yahweh in the way that he desires, particularly following the arrangements that David established, not only will this restore their special identity, they will also help people from all nations come to have faith in Yahweh.

### Who wrote the book of 1 Chronicles?

The author of 1 Chronicles does not state his name, and he does not provide any personal information about himself. So it is not possible to identify who wrote this book.

### What title should translators use for this book?

Translators can use a traditional title such as “The First Book of Chronicles” or “First Chronicles.” They might also call it by a different title such as “The Ancestry and Story of King David.”

### What kind of writing is the book of 1 Chronicles?

Much of the book of 1 Chronicles consists of historical narratives, that is, stories about things that happened in the past. However, the book also contains many lists. There is also a long section of poetry in 16:8–36. Consider how to represent these forms of writing in a way that your readers will appreciate. There are suggestions later in this introduction for how to represent lists.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

## Part 3: Translation Issues in This Book

### Parallel passages with 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings

If you have already translated the books of 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings, that will help you translate this book. The author draws on those books as sources, and he repeats many passages from them, often with only minor changes. Here is a list of the parallels.

1 Chronicles 10:1-12 and 1 Samuel 31:1-13
1 Chronicles 11:1-3 and 2 Samuel 5:1-3
1 Chronicles 11:4-9 and 2 Samuel 5:6-10
1 Chronicles 11:10-47 and 2 Samuel 23:8-39
1 Chronicles 13:1-14 and 2 Samuel 6:1-11
1 Chronicles 14:1-2 and 2 Samuel 5:11-12
1 Chronicles 14:3-7 and 2 Samuel 5:14-16
1 Chronicles 14:8-12 and 2 Samuel 5:17-21
1 Chronicles 14:13-16 and 2 Samuel 5:22-25
1 Chronicles 15:1-16:3 and 2 Samuel 6:12-19
1 Chronicles 16:8-22 and Psalm 105:1-15
1 Chronicles 16:23-33 and Psalm 96:1-13
1 Chronicles 16:34 and Psalm 106:1
1 Chronicles 16:35-36 and Psalm 106:47-48
1 Chronicles 17:1-27 and 2 Samuel 7:1-29
1 Chronicles 18:1-13 and 2 Samuel 8:1-14
1 Chronicles 18:14-17 and 2 Samuel 8:15-18
1 Chronicles 19:1-19 and 2 Samuel 10:1-19
1 Chronicles 20:1 and 2 Samuel 11:1
1 Chronicles 20:1-3 and 2 Samuel 12:26-31
1 Chronicles 20:4-8 and 2 Samuel 21:18-22
1 Chronicles 21:1-27 and 2 Samuel 24:1-25
1 Chronicles 29:23 and 1 Kings 2:12

### Translating names

This book presents many names of people and places. We recommend that in your translation, you spell them the way they sound in your language. However, if a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the spelling that it uses for some common names if that would be more familiar to your readers. For example, a translation in your region might use the name “Solomon,” and you may choose to use that name rather than spelling it “Shelomoh.”

In many cases, the text indicates whether a person is a man (by identifying him as someone’s father, son, or brother) or a woman (by identifying her as someone’s mother, daughter, sister, or wife). Notes will say when a person is a woman if this is not indicated in the text. Otherwise, translators may assume that the person is a man.

In the same way, the text will typically indicate whether a place name is for a city (“And the name of his city: Dinhabah,” 1:43), a region (“the land of Edom,” 1:43), a mountain (“Mount Seir,” 4:42), a river (“the river of Gozan,” 5:26), and so forth. If your language has its own way of expressing the names of particular kinds of places, you should be able to follow these indications to know how to represent such names.

### Formatting lists

There are many lists in this book. They include the series of genealogies in chapters 1–9, the lists of warriors in chapters 11–12, and the lists of priests and Levites and their responsibilities in later chapters. Some of these lists have summary introductions. Some of them have summary conclusions. Some lists have both, and some have neither. In your translation, format the lists in the way that will help your readers understand them best.

For example, you might indent the entire list and put the verse numbers on the left margin. You might put each element of a list on a separate line, and if there are primary and secondary elements (for example, first the name of a father and then a list of his sons), you might put the secondary element on the line below and indent it more than the primary element. When there is an introduction or conclusion, you might indent it the same as a primary element. You might also use section headings to describe the content of each list. In the first two chapters of the book, the ULT models ways to format these lists in order to make their composition simpler to recognize.

## Part 3: Translation Issues in This Book

### “And it happened”

The author often uses the phrase “And it happened” to introduce a new event in the story or a new development within an event. For example, in 10:8, he introduces the development of the Philistines discovering Saul’s body within the event of the battle of Mount Gilboa by saying, “And it happened on the next day that the Philistines came to strip the slain.” To translate this phrase in its various occurrences, use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event or development.

### “behold”

The author and characters often use the word “behold” to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say. While the word literally means “look,” the speakers do not want their listeners to look at something, but to pay careful attention. For example, in 11:1, the leaders of Israel use the term to call David’s attention to their common ancestry and the right they feel he therefore has to rule the whole nation.

### “brothers”

The author and characters often use the term “brothers” to mean not sons of the same father but members of the same nation, tribe, clan, or extended family. For example, in 12:29, the author speaks of the members of the tribe of Benjamin as the “brothers” of Saul. He means that they were his relatives or kinsmen.

### “to this day”

In 1 Chronicles 4:41, 4:43, 5:26, and 13:11, the author uses the phrase “to this day.” He uses the similar phrase “until now” in 9:18. He is drawing on earlier sources that are referring to the time when they were written. Translators should be aware that “to this day” refers to a time that was already in the past when 1 Chronicles was written centuries ago. They must avoid giving the impression that the expression refers to the present day of their own readers. Notes at each instance will suggest how a translation might express the meaning accurately.

### “in the eyes of”

The author and characters often speak of something being good or bad, or right or wrong, “in the eyes of” someone. For example, the author says in 13:4 that when David proposed to bring the Box of Yahweh to Jerusalem, “the matter was right in the eyes of all of the people.” He means that the people considered this the right thing to do.

### “to the face of”

The expression “to the face of” can have different shades of meaning, depending on the context.
* The author and characters often use the word “face” to represent the presence of a person or group, by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present. For example, the author says in 11:3 that the Israelites anointed David as king of Israel “to the face of Yahweh.” He means that they did so in the presence of Yahweh.
* The focus may also be on something being in front of or before a person or thing, in space or in time. For example, the author says in 24:2 that Nadab and Abihu died “to the face of” their father Aaron. He means that they died before he did.
* Sometimes the idea of “in front of” has a further association. For example, the author says in 19:16 that when the Arameans gathered a large army, “Shophach, the commander of the army of Hadadezer, was to their faces.” By saying that Shophach was in front of these troops, he means that he was commanding them.
* The focus may also be on the relationship or interaction between people or groups, as in 11:13, where the author says that the Israelite army “fled from the face of the Philistines.” He means that fled from the Philistines as the Philistines opposed and attacked them.

In other contexts, the author or a character may use the word “face,” describing part of a person, in order to represent the whole person. For example, in 17:25, David tells Yahweh that he has found the courage to pray “to your face.” He is using one part of Yahweh, his “face,” to mean all of him. He means that he has prayed to Yahweh himself.

### “into the hand of”/”into your hand”

The author and characters often use the word “hand” to represent power, capability, or control. For example, David says in 21:13, “into the hand of man, let me not fall.” He is saying that he does not want people, specifically enemy nations, to have power over him and harm him.

The word “hand” may also represent possession or conveyance. The author says in 11:3 that the Israelites anointed David as their king “according to the word of Yahweh by the hand of Samuel.” He is referring to a “word” or message that Samuel brought to the Israelites from Yahweh. The word “hand” may also represent agency. The author describes in 16:7 how David arranged for the Israelites to praise Yahweh “by the hand of Asaph and his brothers,” that is, through the agency of Asaph and his fellow Levites, as they sang and played instruments to lead worship. Notes will help distinguish the difference between these shades of meaning when that may not be clear from the context.

In other contexts, the author or a character may use the word “hand,” describing part of a person, in order to represent the whole person. For example, the author says in 6:15 that the Israelites were exiled “by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.” He is using one part of Nebuchadnezzar, his “hand,” to mean all of him in the act of exiling the Israelites.

### “head”

The author and characters often use the term “head” to mean “leader.” The author says in 11:6 that because Joab led a successful attack against the Jebusites in Jerusalem, “he became the head” of David’s soldiers. He means that he became their leader or commander.

### “house of fathers”

In many places, the author uses the phrase “house of fathers” (or “father’s house”) as a common expression of his culture to describe extended families, comprising three or four generations, led by a man who was the father, grandfather, or great-grandfather of the family members. The household also included servants. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, throughout the book you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning (such as “clans”), or you could state the meaning plainly (as by saying “extended families”).

### “let” and “may”

The ULT uses the English helping verbs “let” and “may” to show that a speaker is expressing a desire that something happen or that someone do something. It uses the verb “let” for more assertive expressions, and it uses the verb “may” for more deferential expressions. For example, when David says in 13:3, “let us bring the Box of our God back to us,” he means, “I want us to bring the Box of our God back to us.” Languages that do not have a volitional form might say, “we ought to bring the Box of our God back to us.” When David tells Solomon in 22:13, “may you not fear,” he is saying what he wants Solomon to do, but he is being more deferential, because he is addressing his own son. Languages that do not have a volitional form might say, “I desire that you not fear,” or they might use an imperative with an indication that it is a polite request, “please do not fear.” Translate this volitional form in the most natural way in your language to indicate that the speaker is expressing what he wishes someone would do.

### “listen”

The author and characters may use the terms “listen” or “hear” to mean complying with what someone has said. For example, the author says in 29:23 that when Solomon became king, “all of Israel listened to him.” He means that the Israelites obeyed Solomon’s commands.

### name of a person representing him and associated or accompanying people

The author and characters often use the name of a person to represent that person and others who are associated with or accompanying that person. For example, in 14:11, when the author says that David struck or defeated the Philistines, he is using David, one person who was involved in this action, to represent everyone who was involved. The text makes clear that it was David and all of his soldiers who did this.

### name of nation, tribe, or city representing its people

The author and characters often use the name of a nation, tribe, or city to represent its people or its army. For example, in 2:7, when the author describes Achar as “the troubler of Israel,” he is using the name of the nation of Israel to mean the people of that nation, the Israelites. (When a nation has the same name as its ancestor, as in this case, this is the same thing as using the name of the ancestor to mean his descendants.)

### “saying”

The author and characters frequently use the term “saying” to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

### “shall”

The ULT represents the Hebrew instructional verb form with the English helping verb “shall.” For example, when David asks in 11:19, using the question form for emphasis, “Shall I drink the blood of these men with their lives?” he means “I should not drink” or “I must not drink.” Translate this form with the most natural way in your language for giving instructions.

### “sons of”

The author and characters often speak of “the sons of” a person to mean the nation or tribe that consists of his descendants. For example, in 19:1, he describes Nahash as the king of the “sons of Ammon.” In such contexts, “sons” does not mean first-generation offspring, but later descendants. The author means that Nahash was the king of the Ammonites.

### “strike/struck”

In many places, the author says that soldiers “struck” an opposing army, city, or king as if they had merely hit them. But he means that they attacked those opponents and usually that they defeated them. That is the case 20:1, where the author says that “Joab struck Rabbah.” He means that Joab and the Israelite army defeated and conquered that city. In some contexts, the specific meaning of “struck” is “killed.” The author describes in 20:4 how, in single combat, Sibbecai the Hushathite “struck” the Philistine giant Sippai. He means that he killed him.

### travel descriptions marked for change in elevation (“went up,” “went down”)

In Hebrew, writers and speakers generally indicated whether people were going up to a higher elevation or going down to a lower elevation when they traveled. For example, in 13:6, the author says that David and the Israelites went to Kiriath Jearim “bring up from there the Box of God.” He says “bring up” because Jerusalem, where David wanted to bring the Box, was higher than Kiriath Jearim. If your language does not generally mark travel for change in elevation, you do not need to do that in your translation.

# 1 Chronicles 1 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the series of genealogies (ancestor lists) that begin with Adam, the first man, and trace the line of his descendants ultimately to David. The genealogies in this chapter go as far as the two sons of Isaac, who were Esau and Israel. One principle of these genealogies is that after introducing a key figure (such as Adam, Noah, Abraham, or Israel), they first trace the line that does not lead toward David, and then they trace the line that does.

1. From Adam to Isaac’s sons Esau and Israel (1–34)
    1. From Adam to Noah and his sons (1–4)
    2. The descendants of Noah’s son Japheth (5–7)
    3. The descendants of Noah’s son Ham (8–16)
    4. The descendants of Noah’s son Shem (17–23)
    5. From Shem to Abraham (24–27)
    6. The descendants of Ishmael (28–31)
    7. The descendants of Abraham’s concubine Keturah (32–33)
    8. The descendants of Abraham’s wife Sarah: Isaac and his sons Esau and Israel (34)
2. The descendants of Esau (35–42)
3. The kings and chiefs of the Edomites, Esau’s descendants (43–54)
    1. The kings of Edom (43–51a)
    2. The chiefs of Edom (51b–54)

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how to format lists so that their composition is simpler to understand. Here are some characteristics of the lists in this chapter. The ULT models ways to format them.

* The list of descendants from Adam to Noah and his sons (1–4) and the list from Shem to Abraham (24–27) each contain ten names, ending with a key figure and providing further information about that figure. It may be helpful to your readers if you format both of these lists in the same way so that they can see this connection.
* The lists of the descendants of Noah’s sons in 5–7, 8–9, and 17 have primary and secondary elements. So do the lists in verses 28–42.
* The list of the kings of Edom in 43–51a has an introductory summary. The lists of Joktan’s, Ishmael’s, and Keturah’s descendants in verses 20–23, 29–31, and 32–33 have concluding summaries. The list of the chiefs of Edom in 51b–54 has an introductory summary and a concluding summary.

# 1 Chronicles 2 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the series of genealogies with which this book begins. In the previous chapter, the genealogies traced the line from Adam to Isaac and his two sons Esau and Israel, and it listed the descendants of Esau. Now the book, in chapters 2–7, will list the descendants of Israel. (The book does not list the descendants of two of Israel’s sons, Dan and Zebulun. Interpreters are not sure why it does not list them.) Judah, the ancestor of the tribe of David, is considered the most important of his sons, and so the list begins by describing Judah’s descendants in this chapter.

1. List of the sons of Israel (1–2)
2. From Judah to his great-grandsons, the sons of Hezron (3–9)
3. The descendants of Hezron’s son Ram, including Jesse and his children (10–17)
4. The descendants of Hezron’s son Caleb (18–19)
5. The descendants of Hezron by his wife, the daughter of Makir (20–23)
6. The descendant of Hezron by his wife Abjijah (24)
7. The descendants of Hezron’s son Jerahmeel (25–41)
8. More descendants of Hezron’s son Caleb (42–48)

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how to format lists so that their composition is simpler to understand. Also see how you formatted the lists in chapter 1 that had various characteristics such as primary and secondary elements, introductory summaries, and concluding summaries. The ULT models ways to format the lists in this chapter.

# 1 Chronicles 4 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the series of genealogies with which this book begins. It continues the description of the twelve tribes descended from Israel that began in chapter 2. It first describes further descendants of Judah. Then it describes the descendants of Simeon. That tribe is grouped with Judah because originally it did not have territory of its own. Instead, the Simeonites lived among the Judeans within their territory, as Joshua 19:9 describes. However, this chapter describes in its last section how they eventually did conquer territory for themselves.

1. Further descendants of Judah (1–23)
    1. An introduction to this section naming five generations of Judah’s descendants (1)
    2. Descendants of Hur (2–4)
    3. Descendants of (Hezron’s son) Ashhur (5–10)
    4. Various other clans of Judah (11–20)
    5. Descendants of Judah’s son Shelah (21–23)
2. The descendants of Simeon (24–43)
    1. A list of Simeon’s direct descendants (24–27)
    2. The cities in which the Simeonites lived (28–33)
    3. Clan leaders of Simeon who conquered more territory for the tribe (34–38)
    4. Description of this conquest (39–43)

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how to format lists so that their composition is simpler to understand. Also see how you formatted the lists in chapters 1 and 2 that had various characteristics such as primary and secondary elements, introductory summaries, and concluding summaries, and see how the ULT models ways to format the lists in those chapters.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The name Jabez

In verse 10, Jabez asks God not to act harmfully toward him “so as not to pain me.” The word that the ULT translates as “pain” comes from a root related to the name Jabez. So Jabez is making a play on words with his own name as he prays to God. In this culture, people believed that a person’s name indicated something that was true about him. (In many cases, a person’s name was changed as a result of something he achieved or something that happened to him.) Although verse 9 explains that the mother of Jabez gave him this name because she bore him after a painful labor, he seems to have been concerned that he would have to deal with poverty and difficult circumstances throughout his life. So by praying in this way, he is asking God to reverse the potential implications of his name. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in a footnote.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Uncertain connections within genealogies

In this chapter, readers encounter for the first time an issue that occurs in many further places in these genealogies. In verse 11, the author identifies Chelub as “the brother of Shuhah,” but he has not previously introduced Shuhah. So it is not clear how Chelub relates to the descendants of Judah whom the author has described. Since this is unknown, we recommend that you not try to account for it in the text of your translation or in a footnote. We recommend that you treat similar instances later in the book in the same way.

# 1 Chronicles 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the series of genealogies with which this book begins. It lists the Israelites who returned from exile in Babylon and settled in Jerusalem. It describes their ancestries and then specifies what the duties of various Levites were. It then repeats the genealogy of Saul from 8:29–38 in order to introduce the story of the Israelite kings that begins with Saul and continues through the rest of this book and through 2 Chronicles.

1. Israelites who resettled Jerusalem after the exile (1–22a)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Michal disdain David for dancing and celebrating?

The author says in 15:29 that as the Israelites were bringing the Box of Yahweh to Jerusalem, David’s wife Michal “saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.” The author does not explain directly why Michal disdained David for doing this. However, he does give a hint in 15:27 when he says that “David was clothed in a robe of fine linen” and “an ephod of linen was on David.” The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 6:14–23 indicates that at some point, probably because he became too warm from dancing, David took off the robe and wore only the ephod. This passage also indicates that, for one thing, Michal felt that this was an inappropriate way for a king to dress. But the author of this book, by not saying that this was the specific reason why Michal disapproved, leaves open the additional possibility that Michal disapproved of David “dancing and celebrating” to honor Yahweh. 1 Samuel 19:13 indicates that Michal had an idol in her home, and it is possible that Michal was not a sincere worshiper of Yahweh. To leave both possibilities similarly open in your translation, we recommend that you not suggest a specific reason why Michal disdained David, either in the text or in a footnote.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Parallels in the Psalms to the song in 16:8–36

Portions of the song that David wrote for the occasion of bringing the Box to Jerusalem constitute all or part of three psalms in the book of Psalms. It seems that those portions were later adapted for use in worship in the temple in the form of these psalms. If you have already translated those psalms, this will help you translate the song here. These are the parallels:
16:8-22 and Psalm 105:1-15
16:23-33 and Psalm 96:1-13
16:34 and Psalm 106:1
16:35-36 and Psalm 106:47-48

### Does 16:38 describe two different men named Obed Edom?

It is possible that 16:38 is describing two different men named Obed Edom and distinguishing between the two by specifying that the second was “the son of Jeduthun.” The first Obed Edom seems to be the one mentioned with Jeiel in 15:18, 15:21, and 16:5. Given how commonly these two are paired, it seems possible that the name “Jeiel” has dropped out of 16:38, which would explain why the author says “their brothers” rather than “his brothers.” The second Obed Edom seems to be the one mentioned in 15:24. It’s possible that Hosah and Jehiah are variant spellings of the same person’s name. It is unclear whether either of these men named Obed Edom is identical with the man by that name described in 13:13–14, in whose house the Box of Yahweh remained for some time. The author describes him as a “Gittite,” but that does not necessarily mean that he was a Philistine from the city of Gath who therefore could not serve in the temple area. This man could have been a Levite who from the Levitical city of Gath-Rimmon, or one who resided in Gath for a time. In either of those cases, he could have been a Levite who was eligible to sing in front of the Box, like the first Obed Edom in 16:38, or to be a gatekeeper, like the second Obed Edom in that verse. Notes address some translation issues related to this question.

### Punctuating the long sentence in verses 37–42

In verses 37–42, the author describes the arrangements David made for perpetual worship at Israel’s holy sites. He begins by saying “And he left” to introduce people whom David stationed in various positions and roles, and then he names those people: Asaph and his relatives (37), Obed Edom and his relatives (38a), Obed Edom and Hosah (38b), Zadok and the priests (39–40), and Heman and Jeduthun (41–42). It may be natural in your language to divide this long sentence into several shorter sentences describing each of these groups of people. The UST models one way to do that.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Multiple levels of quotation in Yahweh’s message to Nathan

Yahweh speaks a message to the prophet Nathan in 4–14. Within this message, there are second-level, third-level, and fourth-level quotations. The entire message is something that Yahweh said and that the author is quoting, so it is a first-level quotation. Within it, Yahweh tells Nathan what he should say, so that is a quotation within a quotation, or a second-level quotation. Yahweh tells Nathan specifically that he should tell David that he has said something, and what he has said is a third-level quotation. Within it, in verse 6, there is a further direct quotation, which is a fourth-level one. Your language may use quotation marks or some other punctuation or convention to indicate various levels of quotation. The ULT models one way to do that. You could also translate the whole message in such a way that there are not quotations within quotations. The UST models one way to do that.

### David referring to himself in the third person

As David responds to the message that Yahweh sent him through the prophet Nathan, he often speaks of himself in the third person as “your servant” to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person throughout these verses. Notes to several verses suggest ways to do that.

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of David. It describes how he defeated the enemy nations that surrounded Israel and took great plunder from them, bringing safety and prosperity to the Israelites. It then gives some details of David’s government administration.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Numbers

There are large numbers in verses 4, 5, and 12. Recall how your team has decided to represent large numbers in your translation.

### “to establish his hand at the River of Euphrates”

In 18:3, the author says that Hadadezer, the ruler of the Aramean kingdom of Zobah Hamath, “went to establish his hand at the River.” Interpreters understand this expression in two main ways. (1) It could mean that Hadadezer led his army against the Israelites in order to ensure that he continued to control his own territory. The kingdom of Zobah lay between the Euphrates River on the east and Israel on the west. Hadadezer may have seen how David had conquered and subdued the Philistines and Moabites, and he may have launched a pre-emptive attack to keep David from conquering him as well. The author may be saying that Hadadezer felt that his authority and control over his territory (his “hand”) had been diminished by David’s military successes against other nations, and so he marched his army out to “establish” control of this area. If you follow this interpretation, you might say in your translation that Hadadezer went out “to assert his control over his territory, from its border with Israel all the way to the Euphrates River.” (2) The expression could also mean that Hadadezer built a monument to himself at the Euphrates River, asserting his control over the territory west of the river, and that he led his army out to set up the monument in order to assert that control. The term “hand” means “monument” in 1 Samuel 15:12, and that could also be the meaning here. However, in this interpretation Hadadezer and his army would have been marching away from Israel and would not necessarily have come into conflict with David. The further implication would have to be that David learned of this action by a hostile king to assert control over his territory, and so he led the Israelite army against him to subdue him. If you follow this interpretation, you might say in your translation that Hadadezer went “to set up a monument to himself at the Euphrates River.”

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Hanun shave half of the beards of David’s messengers and cut their garments in the middle?

In 10:4, to insult David’s messengers, the Ammonite king, Hanun, has his servants shave off half of their beards and cut off half of their robes. In just about any context, these actions would have made the men look foolish and exposed them to shame and embarrassment. But in this culture, there may have been a further significance. In this culture, men wore beards, while women did not have them. By leaving the messengers with half-beards, Hanun was symbolically making them neither men nor women. Humans wear clothes, while animals do not. By leaving the messengers with half-robes, Hanun was symbolically making them neither human nor animal. So this was a way of making the messengers symbolically non-existent. Since they represented David personally, it was a way of insulting David by telling him, “You are nothing.” The author of this book does not explain the significance of this action, since his readers would already have understood it. But if it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain it in a footnote.

### Numbers

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s temple as his “footstool”

When David says in verse 2 that he wanted to build a temple “as a footstool of the feet of our God,” he is using an image that also occurs elsewhere in the Bible. This image envisions heaven as the place of God’s throne and the earth as the place of his footstool, so that God is present on earth as well as in heaven, although in a lesser sense. The psalmist says in 132:7, for example, speaking of going to the temple, “Let us go to his dwellings; let us bow down at the footstool of his feet.”

### Why does the author speak in verse 16 of “tables” for the sacred bread?

Leviticus 24:5–9 describes a single table in front of the lampstand in the tent of meeting for the bread of the arrangement. But according to 2 Chronicles 4:7–8, when Solomon built the temple, he made ten lampstands and ten gold tables to put in front of them. 2 Chronicles 4:19 says that the sacred bread was on these tables. But this was not a departure from what Yahweh wanted. This chapter indicates that it was part of the “plan” that the Spirit of Yahweh revealed to David.
